sources.headline: EU’s new Arctic strategy signals shift in its geopolitical mindset
sources.text:
The EU recently presented its latest Arctic strategy. It is the bloc’s fifth such strategy since 2008 and the first to be published since 2021, a few months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
This conflict has disrupted Arctic governance. The work of the Arctic Council, which includes Russia as one of its eight member states, was paused shortly after the invasion. The council is the primary forum for cooperation in the region.
Since 2022, the Russian security threat in the Arctic has also grown. Russia has engaged in hybrid activities in the region, ranging from disinformation operations and GPS jamming to the targeting of pipelines and undersea cables.
The EU’s new strategy has four priorities: strengthening peace, security and resilience in the Arctic, addressing climate change, delivering economic development and ensuring regional and social development for Arctic communities.
These priorities are broadly in line with the previous 2021 strategy, in which geopolitical issues were already more present than in earlier years. But there are several major changes.
More security and less climate action
A word count reveals the profound impact the deteriorating cooperation context has had on the EU’s stance on the region. In the latest update, the word “security” is mentioned 52 times compared with 23 times in 2021. By contrast, “climate change” appears only 14 times in the new strategy compared with 30 times previously.
This shift towards security is a general trend in the Arctic since 2022. The creation of an annual Arctic Security Conference in 2024, which discusses security trends in the region, is an example of this. Security also figures prominently in recently published national Arctic strategies, including France, Italy, Germany and Sweden.
Climate change is not completely absent from the EU’s latest Arctic strategy, and the bloc reaffirmed its commitment to combat it in the document. But, where previously climate change was the cornerstone of the EU’s Arctic engagement, it is now presented through a security lens. Climate change is identified as “amplifying security risks” and a “defining threat” from which Arctic inhabitants need to be “protected”.
Security shapes all four priorities of the new strategy. Arctic communities also get much more attention than in earlier documents.
Although the inclusion of Indigenous people also figures more prominently, the conflation between Indigenous and local people has previously been criticised by the Saami Council. The conflation undermines the specific rights and distinct interests of Indigenous groups such as the Sámi.
The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, delivers a statement on the EU’s new Arctic strategy at the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on October 20.
Ronald Wittek / EPA
A ‘northern neighbourhood’
Another key change in the EU’s new Arctic strategy is the introduction of the concept of a “northern neighbourhood”. The name suggests similarities with the EU’s European Neighbourhood Policy, which it launched in 2004 to foster closer ties with its eastern and southern neighbours. But it is unclear what exact form the northern neighbourhood will take.
The northern neighbourhood is not presented as a new multilateral institution. Instead, it has been put forward as a political framework enabling cooperation projects and integration between the EU and “like-minded” partners such as Greenland, Norway, Iceland, Canada and the UK.
By excluding Russia, this new political framework signals a change in the EU’s understanding of the Arctic. The EU’s early engagement in the region came from a will to extend European integration to the east and north in the 2000s. The Arctic was also an area where cooperation with Russia was possible, despite disagreements elsewhere.
The concept of a northern neighbourhood reveals a geographical shift in focus towards Greenland and the west and north Atlantic more generally. Yet while the US is still listed among the potential members of the northern neighbourhood, it comes with implicit conditions.
According to the new strategy, a partnership with the US needs to be “predictable” and based on “shared interests and values”. This is reminiscent of the language that prevailed for Russia in the previous policies.
What kind of power is the EU?
Perhaps the biggest change in the new strategy lies in the document’s affirmation that multilateral cooperation “can no longer be the sole foundation of the EU’s Arctic approach”.
This means two things. First, that multilateralism is no longer the prominent form of cooperation in the Arctic. And second, that the EU’s geopolitical stance in general is changing from being the champion and embodiment of multilateralism to another form of power.
This is also visible in the emphasis the new strategy puts on the EU’s material capabilities and infrastructures as conditions for security. It includes mention of, among other things, developing Europe’s capacity to build icebreaker vessels.
The EU’s new Arctic strategy signals a broad shift in the European geopolitical mindset. Climate change and multilateralism have been overshadowed by security concerns due to the fractured Arctic geopolitical landscape.
However, ultimately, climate change and social concerns will remain key priorities of Arctic inhabitants and the EU should not lose sight of this.

sources.headline: The EU and Canada Struggle to Define Their Relationship
sources.text:
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at how deep Canada-EU ties will go, the resignation of European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, and China’s latest political and military purge.
Relationship Status: It’s Complicated
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney hosted senior European Union officials in Montreal on Thursday to discuss bolstering trade and defense ties. Notably downplayed, though, was the EU’s previous offer to make Canada an “associate member” of the 27-nation bloc.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at how deep Canada-EU ties will go, the resignation of European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, and China’s latest political and military purge.
Relationship Status: It’s Complicated
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney hosted senior European Union officials in Montreal on Thursday to discuss bolstering trade and defense ties. Notably downplayed, though, was the EU’s previous offer to make Canada an “associate member” of the 27-nation bloc.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated the idea during her annual State of the European Union address.
“We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said while standing beside Carney. “We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well.” Canadian officials applauded the proposal, with Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador to the EU, saying at the time that Ottawa wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to the bloc.
Yet a statement prepared for this week’s annual Canada-EU summit included a watered-down version of such a future. Rather than explicitly noting the proposed associate member status, the draft text offered “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself,” Politico reported on Wednesday. According to Reuters, a previous draft had included at least two direct mentions of Canada’s associate member status while adding that defining the term would take another year.
“Canada cannot become a full-fledged member of the EU because of geography, but we both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible,” von der Leyen said on Thursday. She described this type of relationship as open “only to our closest partners outside of Europe who are ready to open a new frontier together,” and she stressed that associate member status is not fully off the table.
Von der Leyen’s decision to back off from her full-throated appeal for associate Canadian membership may have been made due to some member nations’ hesitance. Several EU countries, particularly Germany, had argued that they would not approve such a designation, as it had no legal precedent and had not been fully fleshed out. Others accused von der Leyen of not discussing the idea with European leaders first.
“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem,” one diplomat told the Guardian. “This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying.”
The EU’s move to soften the language is likely to appease at least one foreign leader: U.S. President Donald Trump. Trump had called the EU’s initial proposal “laughable” and warned that such a designation could be considered a “hostile act” that could prompt the White House to cut off trade with Europe in certain areas. Already, U.S. trade relations with Canada and the European Union are greatly strained, with Trump repeatedly returning to his tariff war for economic leverage.
Still, Carney appeared to be unconcerned by Thursday’s language shift. “The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”
Today’s Most Read
Dramatic Changes Are Unlikely in Israel, Even if Netanyahu Is Ousted by Steven A. Cook
How to Not Change Your Mind by Stephen M. Walt
Dawn of the Data Centers by Christina Lu
What We’re Following
Who will run the ECB next? European Central Bank (ECB) President Christine Lagarde announced on Thursday that she will step down from her role in February, officially triggering a race to determine who will take up the mantle of one of the European Union’s top posts. Her eight-year term was set to end in October 2027; her early departure allows the EU to choose her successor before one of its members, France, holds a consequential presidential election that could upset the bloc’s balance.
In April, France will hold a highly anticipated presidential vote that could see far-right National Rally candidate Marine Le Pen take power. Eurozone members had worried that a Le Pen victory could affect who is selected to be the new ECB president, as the populist lawmaker has previously criticized EU financial institutions and expressed disinterest in choosing another mainstream central banker to lead the body. Lagarde resigning early therefore allows outgoing French President Emmanuel Macron to have a say in her replacement instead.
Among the front-runners for Lagarde’s post are former Spanish Central Bank head Pablo Hernández de Cos and former Dutch Central Bank chief Klaas Knot. Whoever is chosen will have to contend with energy price shocks, bond market turmoil, and persistent high inflation.
Meanwhile, it is unclear what’s next for Lagarde, who was the first woman to serve as the ECB president. “I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression, and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters,” Lagarde said on Thursday. Some analysts believe that Lagarde, who is a French citizen, aims to become more vocal in the country’s politics, which have faced weeks of upheaval due to sweeping student-led protests.
Xi’s latest purge. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) confirmed the expulsion of 33 senior political and military officials on Thursday, in one of President Xi Jinping’s most sweeping purges since taking office in 2012. Those removed include Liu Jianchao, the former head of the CCP’s International Department; former Politburo member Ma Xingrui; Zhang Youxia, once the country’s most senior general; and Zhong Shaojun, a top military secretary to Xi.
It is unclear what charges these members faced beyond “serious disciplinary and legal violations.” But the expulsions are part of Xi’s extensive anti-corruption campaign targeting those considered disloyal to the party, and it comes as the longtime leader is preparing to clinch a fourth term in office. “While maintaining a tough stance against corruption, we should also strengthen checks on and oversight over the exercise of power,” read a communiqué released by the CCP’s Central Committee on Thursday.
The announcement concluded this year’s multiday Central Committee meeting in Beijing. Only 279 officials attended the annual conference, compared to 376 members when the current body was formed in 2022. This was the first time during Xi’s term that the plenary’s attendance dropped below 300 people. That suggests that nearly 100 officials were likely purged from the party over the course of just four years, China experts say.
National mourning. Spanish search-and-rescue operations stretched into Thursday following a deadly high-speed train crash the day before. At least 69 deaths have been confirmed thus far, with some 50 individuals still hospitalized, and local authorities fear that the death toll could rise. Madrid declared three days of national mourning starting Thursday.
Early Wednesday, a high-speed passenger train believed to be going around 120 miles per hour slammed into a stopped train near the central Spanish city of Toledo. An initial investigation found that an information technology failure involving railroad switching equipment was to blame. However, critics have accused the Spanish government of failing to provide adequate oversight and maintenance of the world’s second-largest high-speed rail network, particularly after another train crash on the same line killed 46 people in January.
“It is clear that we need to reinforce the safety of our train service to rebuild the trust in our high-speed rail,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Wednesday. “It is not acceptable for a country like Spain to endure two high-speed train accidents in the same year.” With the country holding snap parliamentary elections next month, public transportation reform will likely be a top concern among voters.
Odds and Ends
The Vatican Museums opened a new exhibition on Thursday that celebrates more than 100 years of papal travel. Dubbed “A Century of the Popemobile,” the showing features eight Mercedes-Benz vehicles that popes have used since 1930 to travel among the faithful. Notable design alterations include Pope John XXIII’s 300 d Landaulet, which included removable rear side windows to allow the pontiff to reach out to those he passed on the road, and Pope John Paul II’s 230 G, which added the car’s transparent dome for greater viewing access.

sources.headline: Europe Was Never Meant to Be a ‘Regulatory Superpower’
sources.text:
Over the decades, the European Union has weathered recessions and revolutions, internal fissures and external threats. It has seen the Iron Curtain teeter and fall and watched as the world order shifted from bipolar to unipolar to something else entirely. Through it all, the EU has proved remarkably durable, but threats loom on the horizon.
The EU now faces a dizzying array of challenges. To the east, Russia’s grinding invasion of Ukraine strains European budgets, imperils fragile supply chains, and jeopardizes the longevity of the European project. Across the Atlantic, meanwhile, Washington has adopted a challenging stance on a variety of issues, placing mounting pressure on the trans-Atlantic relationship. China’s use of predatory economics threatens the old continent’s export industry and its economic model. Over the decades, the European Union has weathered recessions and revolutions, internal fissures and external threats. It has seen the Iron Curtain teeter and fall and watched as the world order shifted from bipolar to unipolar to something else entirely. Through it all, the EU has proved remarkably durable, but threats loom on the horizon.
The EU now faces a dizzying array of challenges. To the east, Russia’s grinding invasion of Ukraine strains European budgets, imperils fragile supply chains, and jeopardizes the longevity of the European project. Across the Atlantic, meanwhile, Washington has adopted a challenging stance on a variety of issues, placing mounting pressure on the trans-Atlantic relationship. China’s use of predatory economics threatens the old continent’s export industry and its economic model. And economic stagnation, soaring energy prices, and an ongoing migration crisis have further corroded European cohesion, contributing to widespread dissatisfaction and mounting distrust.
These developments have left the EU in a precarious position. While the grouping was once a leading force in the global economy, decades of lax industrial policy and heavy regulations have eroded its influence. As recently as 1980, the 27 EU member states collectively accounted for approximately 34 percent of global GDP. Industrial output remains anemic, while the European tech sector continues to lag well behind foreign competitors, and productivity slows year on year.
In response, Brussels has fallen back on familiar logic. Rather than embracing uncertainty, the EU has sought to reassert control over it by turning once again to its vaunted regulatory ecosystem. For many European leaders, the continent’s strength lies not in military might or industrial productivity but in its ability to shape global rules and standards. The bloc has increasingly been described as a “regulatory superpower,” capable of projecting its normative power far beyond its borders. International trade expert Anu Bradford has dubbed this concept the “Brussels Effect,” arguing that regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act have given the EU outsized influence over international economic standards. Advocates of this vision argue that for countries and companies interested in accessing the continent’s vast and wealthy internal market, adapting to European regulations is a small price to pay. European Commission Vice President Teresa Ribera went so far as to say these rules are “non-negotiable.”
But Robert Schuman and the EU’s founding fathers never intended to build a union focused on bringing companies to their knees—rather, they wanted to build one capable of standing up to foreign adversaries. The regulatory approach is outdated, too. Thankfully, the EU has another, even more potent tool in its arsenal: trade.
In its earliest incarnation—the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC)—the EU was almost exclusively an economic construct. The ECSC and its successor, the European Economic Community, were built primarily to amplify European economic influence by linking and coordinating the continent’s diverse economies. Individually, member states were relatively inconsequential; as a collective, they were a force to be reckoned with. But as the EU has matured, national leaders deprioritized competitiveness, and the bloc’s economic dynamism has dwindled. Many leading European firms have grown sclerotic with age, resting on historical legacies while foreign counterparts have surged ahead. And despite EU efforts to build a thriving start-up ecosystem, byzantine regulatory regimes and heavy tax burdens have continued to hamper growth. Brussels has lost its edge, and regulations are not the solution.
Meanwhile, the United States has abandoned global rules it deems obstacles to its own prosperity. It has replaced multilateral committees with bilateral dealmaking, de facto free trade with a realist-inspired industrial policy. U.S. tech firms have been empowered to act as implements of American power, becoming formidable international actors in their own right. Against this backdrop, the EU’s outdated commitment to red tape and regulations is potentially more of a burden than a boon.
According to the International Monetary Fund, red tape in the EU acts as a hidden tax, amounting to 44 percent on goods and up to 110 percent on services. Similarly, a recent report by the Information Technology & Innovation Foundation estimated that EU regulations have cost European businesses about $176 billion annually, equivalent to nearly 1 percent of collective GDP. Former Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi railed against overzealous regulation in his 2024 report.
Organizations and governments do not have to choose between regulation and trade. In the age of AI, Europe’s regulatory skill could be an asset. But European states still have to choose what to prioritize and where to allocate finite political capital. Rather than doubling down on rule-making, Brussels should work to more effectively bring its vast economic resources to bear.
Indeed, it can be easy to overlook the EU’s massive economic footprint. Collectively, the bloc’s economy ranks as the world’s Its 27 member states boast a combined population of more than 450 million, accounting for approximately 5.5 percent of the global population. By international standards, EU citizens are exceedingly wealthy, controlling a total household income of some in 2024. This vast and affluent pool of consumers has made the EU an irresistible target for international trade partners.
By most metrics, the EU is the world’s largest trade power. Accounting for 16 percent of total world trade in goods and services, the bloc . Brussels currently maintains 45 trade agreements with more than 80 countries and territories from Mercosur to Indonesia. Collectively, these agreements encompass more than 2 billion people and a combined GDP in the tens of trillions of dollars. By some estimates, the EU’s trade network accounts for upwards of 52 percent of global trade.
Despite its immense economic importance, the EU has increasingly found itself on the outside looking in, particularly since the 2008 global financial crisis. To remedy this, European leaders have proposed a raft of reforms. A growing contingent has advocated for increased European defense integration, including massive investments in defense manufacturing and interoperability.
Some political leaders have argued that investing in the continent’s underdeveloped defense industrial base through an EU Defense Union can not only prepare Europe for conflict but also catalyze investment and create new jobs. This analysis is correct, but it is ultimately a long-term solution to an urgent, short-term problem. Reinvigorating Europe’s defense sector alone will not fix a stagnant economy. The political cost would be exceedingly high, while reactivating factories and building new armed forces could take well over a decade. The truth of the matter is that the EU was never intended to be a defense alliance, as failed negotiations on the subject in the 1950s and 1980s can attest.
The EU’s founders believed that by pooling together the industries of their individual countries, they could stand tall against foreign pressure, particularly from the Soviet Union. The European leaders of today should seize that same mentality to become a trade superpower, becoming a source of certainty, fair trade, and investment in an ever more uncertain and fractured world.
By signing new trade agreements with major economies in Africa and creating investment vehicles for infrastructure in emerging economies, Europe can become the world’s partner of choice. Importantly, the EU should promulgate a new trade architecture that seeks to a) connect opposing blocs; b) secure critical minerals and needed resources; c) invest in partners’ trade infrastructure; and d) expand trade agreements with existing partners and sign new ones. The EU free trade agreements with India and Mercosur, signed earlier this year, are two excellent steps in this direction.
This new strategy, however, should include distinct approaches for exports and imports.
The EU is heavily exposed to China for its rare-earth consumption, with Beijing supplying . To reduce this dependence, Brussels should proactively pursue bilateral mineral agreements with resource-rich nations, such as the Philippines, Indonesia, or Mexico. The goal should go beyond importing raw ore to be processed in Europe, to invest in those countries’ refining capacity. By doing so with dozens of mineral-rich countries, the EU could become the main trading house for critical minerals, leveraging a network of free trade agreements without parallel. By doing so, Brussels would develop significant influence in ensuring prices remain stable and advantageous to European interests. The Global Gateway, an EU program seeking to challenge China’s Belt and Road Initiative, is already poised to be the main vehicle for this proposal. To be clear, the EU should avoid any temptation to engage in predatory “resource colonialism.” Instead, this new strategy would treat resource-rich nations as equal partners, channeling investments into their territories to refine minerals there while granting market access in return.
On the export side, however, Europe still has great strengths to contribute to the global economy. Brussels would be wise to leverage them. The developing world has a growing need for readily available capital and credit from trustworthy institutions. Africa and Latin America have the highest percentages of unbanked populations in the world. European banks, many of which already have operations in these regions, should be empowered to expand operations, providing the capital that will unlock future prosperity. Through a combination of bilateral financing and capital deals with those countries, the agreement of standards under a new Basel agreement, and the creation of a Savings and Investments Union, the EU can strip away the red tape that currently holds these firms back. Doing so would bolster Europe’s banking sector while cementing its role as a financial powerhouse.
The same is true for chemicals, pharmaceutical ingredients, and heavy machinery. All of these industries are led by historic European firms, and they are the base of advanced industry, export capacity, and future prosperity. To maximize the effectiveness of its industrial champions, however, European capitals must first complete the Single Market and allow for the free movement of capital, investments, and banks.
Choosing this new path will require a shift in mentality in Brussels. For decades, policymakers have sought power in regulating the economy. Now, they must choose to lead it. sources.headline: Can EU and India work together to secure Indo-Pacific?
sources.text:
The European Union is vying for a larger role in Indo-Pacific security as the US finds itself on the back foot in the Eastern Hemisphere.
India is among the regional powers looking for new allies. Its rising economy and increasingly global ambitions have pushed it into new forums and partnerships, including ever closer defense ties with the European bloc.
In January this year, India and the EU signed a Security and Defense Partnership, followed by their first formal Security and Defense Dialogue in March. More meetings followed throughout the year, including the fifth Maritime Security Dialogue in Brussels last month.
However, while both sides want to boost cooperation on maritime security, working together in the Indo-Pacific remains a challenge — India and European countries simply have different defense priorities.
France a player in the Indian Ocean theater
"Europe can be a credible defense partner of India, especially in the maritime theater in general and Indo-Pacific in particular," Mohan Kumar, a former Indian ambassador to France, told DW.
But Europe's capacity to expand its role is constrained by other security crises.
"European distractions such as the conflict in Ukraine, which is of existential importance for it, do detract from this objective and can be a limiting factor," he added.
How Europe's defense sector is trying to gear upTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
France is a notable exception, given its established military presence in the Indian Ocean.
"France, with its presence in Reunion Island and Mayotte, is already cooperating with India in the Indian Ocean theater and this cooperation can be intensified," added Kumar.
Javed Ashraf, another Indian diplomat, said that France has been "a strong, trusted and consistent security partner across the full spectrum of defense cooperation."
"What makes the partnership easier is the acceptance that the two may not always agree or be in a position to cooperate," said Ashraf.
"France also stands out for India because [France] has currently no defense cooperation with Pakistan or with China."
EU disunited on security?
While France remains the EU's only nuclear power and maintains its strongest military force, a cooperation between Paris and New Delhi does not automatically translate into a coherent European security role across the Indo-Pacific.
"Europe as an entity has very little role in the Indo-Pacific security despite the announcement of a strategy in 2025," said Tara Kartha, a former member of India's National Security Council Secretariat.
She pointed to political differences among EU members as an obstacle to a coherent security outlook.
Those differences were on display during the EU's October 15–16 summit in Brussels, when leaders reaffirmed support for Ukraine, but also signaled disagreements over funding and national priorities.What can EU offer to India?
This could also explain why, as India's defense ties with Europe keep expanding, much of that cooperation still takes place between New Delhi and individual European nations.
Germany, Spain, Italy and Poland have all emerged as important partners.
Why India wants German submarinesTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Ashraf said Brussels could signal broader support for its member states' partnerships with India and provide access to EU-funded programs, boosting cooperation in areas such as maritime security, space, critical minerals, chips and defense technologies.
"India is also becoming an important source of defense supplies for a re-arming Europe," the diplomat added.
There may also be opportunities to share experience in emerging areas of warfare.
"India could also access drone technology in light of valuable experience gained by Europeans in Ukraine," Kumar said.
Germany, the EU's largest economy, is another important part of this relationship. Alongside France, it has become a defense partner for India, including through major equipment purchases. India could push for its relationship with Berlin to include industrial partnerships and technology development.
But experts warn that closer defense ties should not be confused with a shared strategic outlook, as European countries have their own priorities.
Russia and China as major obstacles
The differences between Brussels and New Delhi are particularly clear when it comes to Russia and China.
India still relies heavily on Russian equipment and technology, even as it seeks to diversify its defense supplies. European governments, meanwhile, have been engaged in a tense standoff with Russia since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
How India has become Russia's trade lifelineTo view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
That creates a problem for those seeking to deepen defense industry ties.
"Buying a few big-ticket defense items, such as Rafale fighter jets from France or submarines from Germany, is one thing," said Gulshan Sachdeva, a professor of European Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi.
"However, integrating India's defense industry into the expanding European defense value chain is more challenging as long as Russia remains Europe's principal security concern."
China presents a different but equally important challenge. For India, China is a rival and source of major security issues, including an ongoing border dispute. While the EU also sees China as a "systemic rival," its members differ in how they balance security concerns with their economic relationships with China.
These differences complicate attempts to develop a shared assessment of Indo-Pacific threats.
On a geopolitical level, India wants partnerships that strengthen its capabilities without requiring it to align fully with another power's strategic priorities. European governments are also weighing their regional ambitions against security demands closer to home.The US has moved much of its naval power out of the Indo-Pacific due to the conflicts in the Middle EastImage: U.S. Navy/ZUMA/picture alliance
Cooperation without a security umbrella
The new India-EU partnership creates a framework for closer engagement, but it does not amount to a joint security commitment.
Ashraf said the two sides could strengthen their mutual capabilities but were unlikely to exercise a visible influence on the global security order.
For now, maritime domain awareness, information-sharing, defense technology and selective industrial cooperation offer more realistic prospects than a common security role of the EU and India across the Indo-Pacific.

sources.headline: 70 years ago the Suez crisis exposed British relative decline. Today, the Iran conflict could be doing the same for the US
sources.text:
Months after the US and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran, the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed. The UK chose not to get directly involved in the conflict. Nonetheless, it has been exposed to the crisis through record-high diesel prices as well as a spike in inflation.
This echoes an earlier crisis in the Middle East, as my recent research illustrates.
Seventy years ago, the Egyptian government nationalised the Suez canal, sparking the Suez crisis. The canal, which passes through Egypt from the Red Sea to the Mediterranean, was a vital link for ships travelling between Europe and Asia.
After its completion in 1869 by a French-led company, the Egyptian government held a 44% stake in it. However, financial difficulties forced Egypt to sell its shares to the British government in 1875, leaving Britain and France with substantial financial interests in the canal.
Following the Egyptian nationalisation of the canal, France and Britain – together with Israel – invaded Egypt in an attempt to regain control of the vital waterway. But the invasion was a spectacular failure that was condemned by the international community. The crisis came to symbolise Britain’s loss of superpower status.
Today, the US midterm elections are increasing the pressure on the Trump administration over the current conflict. Elections in Israel have also had some bearing on the conflict, with recent reports that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushed for renewed strikes ahead of the election. Other reports suggest that the US and Israel have drawn up plans to resume strikes after the elections.
In 1956, US presidential elections were also an important part of the calculus. But back then, Britain and France had assumed that the elections would distract the US from their actions. This was a miscalculation. In communication with UK Prime Minister Anthony Eden the day after the vote, US President Dwight D. Eisenhower was clear that his administration would not tolerate the UK, France and Israel’s continued actions. He demanded a negotiated settlement through the UN.
The parallels between Suez and Hormuz go beyond the closure of two vital waterways. Both crises raise the same question: how far can geopolitical power outrun economic power?
Superpowers in decline
In 1944, the American foreign policy professor William T.R. Fox coined the term “super-power”. He defined it as the consequence of “great wealth, great population, and favourable geographic position”. This is similar to how the historian Phillips O’Brien defines great power today. Fox saw three superpowers at that time: the US, Britain, and the Soviet Union. He later acknowledged that including Britain had been a mistake, primarily because of its relative decline against the US and later the rest of Europe.
Arguably a similar shift is taking place today.
There are arguments over what is the best measure of an economy, but on the basis of purchasing power the shift is striking. China has moved from being a fraction of the size of the US economy in 1990 to being well ahead today.
In the 19th century, Britain was the dominant global power and benefited from what economists call “exorbitant privilege”. This was the ability to easily finance debt at favourable interest rates because sterling played a central role in the international monetary system. London was also the world’s leading financial centre.
But as Britain declined, this privilege gradually shifted towards the US. Its loss became particularly pressing during the Suez crisis as the pound came under intense pressure. Similarly today, there are signs of strain in the financial system that underpins American power.
During the Suez crisis, Britain’s currency weakness and dependence on American financial support constrained its ability to act independently, despite its considerable military power.
The crisis was also part of wider cold war geopolitics. An arms deal signed in 1955 between Egypt and the Soviet Union had upset the regional balance of power and contributed to Israel’s decision to get involved in a preventative war.
In response to the arms deal, the US withdrew financing for the Aswan Dam, a major infrastructure project on the River Nile. Then, in 1956, Egypt nationalised the Suez canal, sparking the crisis. British leaders sought to portray Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser as a 1930s dictator, intent on regional dominance.
Egyptian president Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal in 1956.
Wikimedia Commons
The US intervention in Iran has similar connotations. US secretary of war Pete Hegseth has presented the assassination of the Iranian leadership as necessary to prevent an existential threat from “America’s mortal enemy”.
Geoeconomics, the relationship between economics and geopolitics, also played a central role in the Suez crisis. The canal was a major conduit for Middle Eastern oil and there were fears that the nationalisation of the canal would disrupt UK oil supplies. But ironically, it was the decision to invade Egypt that led to a shortage of oil and fuel rationing in the UK.
The wider cold war was a key factor in the US stance on events. The US did not want to be seen to be condoning imperial actions in Egypt while condemning Russian imperialism in Hungary. Just as the Suez crisis needs to be understood in the context of the cold war, the current conflict should also be seen through the lens of “cold war II” geopolitics. Relations between the US and China have not thawed, while proxy wars bear similarities to the first cold war.
Today, the US is increasingly stretched, most clearly seen in the depletion of its munitions. These were already under pressure (in part because of its support for Ukraine) and have been further reduced by the war with Iran.
The Suez crisis illustrates how political leaders can be slow to appreciate the economic constraints on their geopolitical ambitions. The US today is not Britain in 1956, yet the conflict in Iran has prompted questions about the limits of American power. As its relative economic dominance is challenged, will the US also have to reconsider the extent of its global military commitments?

sources.headline: Why over two-thirds of Americans say their country is in decline
sources.text:
Inflation is causing real economic pain. Worries about healthcare costs have jumped sharply. And 7 in 10 Americans believe the country is in decline.
That is the landscape for the 2026 midterm election, according to a new survey from the American Communities Project at Michigan State University, which I direct.
The findings, which follow up previous data work the American Communities Project has done in 2023, 2024 and 2025, come from a survey of 2,155 American adults over two weeks in September 2026, conducted by the survey research firm SSRS, using an online panel and telephone, with a margin of error of +/- 2.4 percentage points.
The American Communities Project studies 15 types of communities. Taken as a whole, the national numbers reveal an electorate that is unsettled, gloomy and likely looking for change.
Inflation: Deepening concern
Cost of living is a unifying concern for all Americans. For the past four years, when given a list of 20 issues – including abortion, climate change, gun violence, drug addiction, education, healthcare, housing, immigration and taxes – respondents have consistently reported that inflation is the No. 1 issue in their community.
But the new data shows something more significant. Almost half of Americans, 47%, say they are experiencing real pain from rising prices – a sharp rise from previous years.
In 2023, 2025 and 2026, we asked respondents whether they were experiencing “serious financial problems” due to price increases. In July 2023, 27% answered yes. In 2025, 30% said yes. In 2026, 47% said yes. This significant swing underscores that many Americans across the country are really hurting in this economy.
For some groups, concern about costs reached well above 50%. For those ages 18-29 – members of Gen Z – 61% said they are dealing with serious financial problems because of price increases, the highest percentage among the four generational cohorts, including ages 30-49, 50-64 and 65+.
Cost of living was also a particular concern reported among people of color. Overall, 65% of Hispanics and 63% of Black Americans said they are experiencing serious financial problems because of price increases.
Healthcare: A rising issue
Healthcare emerged as a top issue in our new survey.
In 2025, 20% of respondents said it was a top concern in their community. This year, 30% cited healthcare as a top concern, a 10-point jump. That shift also made healthcare the No. 2 issue in this survey, after inflation.
For some demographic groups, concern about healthcare in their community reached above one-third of respondents. Among those whose income falls between US$75,000 and $99,999, 36% said healthcare is a top issue; among Black Americans, 35% said so.
This tracks with the policy changes and public health challenges since our 2025 survey. Many have lost health insurance, hospitals have closed, and disease outbreaks have affected communities.
It also may be tied to increasing costs overall. The pain people feel from inflation in healthcare can be especially acute because the dollar amounts can be large.
The United States in decline
The 2026 survey data also showed a 15-point jump in the percentage of Americans who agree with the statement: The United States is in decline. The number is at 70% this year, up from 55% in 2025.
In some ways that number makes sense. Consider the other numbers mentioned here – pain from inflation and concerns about healthcare – and the mood of Americans in general.
But there is another important point in the data. That number, 70%, is exactly what it was in 2023, the first year the American Communities Project did a survey. In 2025, the “decline” number dropped to 55%, and that change was largely driven by communities that voted for President Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election.
It was a measure of hope for the future, and it showed in massive improvements in the general hopefulness in communities such as the evangelical hubs, concentrated heavily in the South, rural middle America and the middle suburbs.
The fact that the “decline” number is back to 70% suggests those same Trump-supporting communities have seen their hopes take a hit – and a deeper analysis of the data on the American Communities Project website shows just that.
At the very least, the data suggests a very disillusioned electorate.
Times and attitudes change
It’s important to keep the 2024 election in mind as the 2026 midterm elections near. It’s a sign of how opinions and attitudes can change – and quickly.
The data here represents this moment in time, and it will likely move after November, which is why we will field this same survey again after the new Congress is seated.
On Oct. 26 we released our more detailed community-level findings on the American Communities Project website. This data explores how opinions and attitudes differ depending on where and how people live.

sources.headline: No One Has a Plan for American Decline
sources.text:
America’s geopolitical power is crumbling, and that shouldn’t be too much of a surprise. Hegemons, after all, rise and fall. Yet nobody in U.S. politics or punditry seems to actually want to talk about the consequences, especially for the American people. When it comes to decline, they either believe it won’t happen or won’t matter—in other words, that America can’t decline or that Americans will be just fine if it does.
Many in the neoconservative and traditionally conservative wings of the Republican Party believe that with the renewed application of its still considerable military and political power, America can remain the world’s dominant power for the foreseeable future. Republican restrainers, in turn, believe that if America forsakes dominance and conserves its power, global disorder can be kept at bay and the American people will be better for it. And while key figures in President Donald Trump’s orbit are all too worried about decline in racial or civilizational terms, they have their own dangerous and counterproductive ideas for how to reverse it.
On the Democratic side, many in the more traditional, liberal internationalist wing of the party maintain, with more modesty than their neoconservative counterparts, that Washington can still lead the way in renewing a global order that will broadly serve U.S. interests. Finally, the progressive wing of the party is convinced that a more restrained foreign policy will bring peace to the world and prosperity to ordinary voters, with the only negative consequences borne by the billionaire class.
But what if everyone’s right about the wrong things? The worst possible outcome would be if the restrainers prove correct about the fact that sustaining America’s global preeminence is no longer possible, and the neocons and liberal internationalists prove right about all the bad results. What if ordinary Americans really did benefit from the unique international stature of the United States, and will sorely miss it when it’s gone?
A crowd of demonstrators marches along a city street lined with tall buildings, with a large cardboard protest sign reading "People Over Billionaires" held prominently in the foreground.
A protester holding a cardboard sign that reads “People Over Billionaires” takes part in a national day of protest in New York on March 28. Jerome Gilles/NurPhoto via Getty Images
Much as Trump’s presidency has served as a catalyst for American decline, his open disdain for the U.S. foreign-policy consensus has catalyzed the debate over what went wrong and what comes next.
Committed champions of Washington’s traditional foreign policy lament that voters no longer seem to support American global leadership. On the other side, many progressives and pro-restraint conservatives have argued that, however duplicitously, Trump channeled the public’s justified anger over Washington’s failed commitment to global hegemony.
But there’s an alternative, more worrying, story about what Americans really gained from their country’s unprecedented geopolitical power and why they concluded these gains were no longer being realized.
Over the course of the Cold War, and all the more so immediately after, U.S. foreign policy largely delivered voters the benefits of hegemony—both material and psychological—without the cost of extensive foreign wars.
In both good ways and bad, U.S. power helped underpin an extraordinary expansion of global trade and industrialization from which America and Americans grew wealthy. Washington defended democratic stability in Europe through NATO and imposed autocratic stability through friendly dictators in the Middle East. It used its economic power to help allies industrialize on America’s terms and push recalcitrant governments to open their markets, while using military force to secure the freedom of the seas and prevent other governments from industrializing on their own terms.
Meanwhile, the dynamism and independence of American education, combined with massive military spending and an apocalyptic arms race, helped drive unprecedented scientific breakthroughs.
Partially as a result of all this, America’s real GDP has grown more than tenfold since 1945. These gains have not been shared equally by the country’s population. But the period of postwar prosperity and broad-based economic growth also helped maintain public support for expanded government programs and a strong social safety net.
Meanwhile, Washington’s preponderance of power often enabled it to impose its will through pressure and proxy wars rather than direct military conflict. Other people paid the cost of American power, often in blood. While wars like Vietnam and Iraq took a violent toll on Americans, they took a far worse one on Vietnamese and Iraqis.
Now, however, that hegemony is waning—and so are the benefits. The financial gains from America’s position have increasingly accrued to a small and wealthy elite, while the prestige has accrued to a community that many Americans no longer identify with. As a result, voters now feel like they are paying the price of U.S. power without reaping its rewards.
Americans remain awkward about acknowledging the benefits of empire, and thus the price of losing it. Many neoconservatives and liberal internationalists are more comfortable discussing the freedom and prosperity American power brings the world. Trump and many others on the anti-internationalist right have taken the selfless side of this rhetoric at face value, suggesting that Americans are suckers for underwriting the world’s well-being free of charge.
Those on the left, by contrast, have been happy to highlight the material benefits of U.S. power. Progressive critiques have long reduced U.S. foreign policy to a neo-imperial bid for markets to exploit. But in this telling, the profits only ever accrued to big corporations, not ordinary Americans. Trump and the left might disagree on whether the plutocrats benefit from U.S. global hegemony, but they fundamentally agree that the rest of the country doesn’t. From this perspective, a more restrained foreign policy that accepts, even embraces, America’s smaller role in a more multipolar world brings considerable savings and no consequences.
Yet the reality may be this: During the heyday of postwar American foreign policy, the country’s role in the world really did bring widespread economic rewards to all Americans. But due to changes in the global order, there is no possible foreign policy that can bring these benefits back in the same way today. It is, at the very least, a possibility policymakers should be planning for.
Two men wearing dark suits stand talking outdoors on a tarmac, with military and private airplanes visible in the blurred background.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth step off Air Force One upon arrival at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware to attend a dignified transfer on March 18 for six U.S. military members who were killed in the Middle East. Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images
Mitigating the material consequences of American decline, however difficult, may still prove far easier than mitigating the psychological consequences. A lot of Americans derived a real sense of pride and security from their country’s preeminent position. Power conferred a sense of prestige, and also a sense of control over a chaotic world.
Since at least 1945, America’s national image has been wrapped up in its wealth and military might, but also, for Republicans and Democrats alike, its role as a respected leader, reliable ally, and generous benefactor. Trump rejected this tradition, but his presidency has been a continuous appeal to Americans’ deep desire for a lost feeling of power and control.
America’s victory in World War II offered the country a heady combination of both military glory and genuine respect. In the ensuing decades, ordinary Americans who traveled abroad, whether as service members, peace corps volunteers, government employees, tourists, or businesspeople—got to bathe in this. In politics, economics, and culture, Americans mattered more because America mattered. At the very least, they could safely assume that everyone in the world wanted to talk about American movies, American TV, and American music.
The country’s reputation became more controversial over time. But America, and by extension Americans abroad, still warranted a great deal of attention. Even people who never traveled saw their presidents and generals receive the world’s deference and were able to partake vicariously. But just as American power was peaking at the start of the new millennium, a mix of partisan culture war and racism changed the relationship between many Americans and their country’s international image. Unlike in the Cold War, the people representing America on TV, making foreign policy and talking about it, became both more liberal and less white than they’d been before.
This means that for Trump and his movement, responsible liberal internationalism delivered respect to the wrong people, and they no longer saw their country’s prestige as their own. Conservatives complained about President Barack Obama’s global “apology tour” while watching him receive the Nobel Peace Prize and international praise. Trump promised to fix this by, in David Frum’s words, “redistributing respect away from those who command too much (overeducated coastal elites) to those who don’t have enough (white Americans without advanced degrees who feel left behind).” Where once diplomats, aid workers, and journalists got careers that delivered a sense of stature, Trump would leave them crying outside of their offices, whether at the State Department, the U.S. Agency for International Development, or Voice of America.
To complete the redistribution, Trump’s policies would then bring a different set of psychological rewards to a different constituency. Instead of the “liberal-professional preference for restrained institutional blandness,” he offered “gilding,” “military fanfare,” and “inflated talk of seizure and possession.” This was a form of national strength Trump’s followers could partake in. Or, as the president himself said in explaining why he wanted to seize Greenland: “[W]hat I feel is psychologically needed for success.”
A weathered, vintage fuel pump displaying an unleaded price sign stands outdoors, with an American flag visible in the soft-focus background.
A U.S. flag hangs from a gas pump in Allagash, Maine, on Oct. 14. Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images
Over the course of the 20th century, Americans have gotten accustomed to global power and to exercising it on the cheap. No one has a plan for what happens when this is no longer possible.
When events ranging from terrorist attacks to foreign wars threaten their sense of security, voters expect their leaders to respond in a way that restores some sense of control. Thus, while Americans may have been genuinely sick of the Iraq War, and genuinely opposed to intervening in Syria, when the Islamic State started beheading people on TV, they demanded that Obama do something.
So far, Trump has been able to meet this expectation by spending down the military, diplomatic, and economic power that the U.S. accumulated through decades of responsible, or at least less reckless, policymaking. Flouting international law to bring Venezuela’s president to New York in shackles was a true testament to American military prowess. And the photos undoubtedly brought some viewers the same satisfaction Romans felt watching enemy leaders led by in a triumphal parade. But the Iran war quickly demonstrated the limits of Trump’s approach.
Already, Iran’s ability to defy Washington for eight months has had a direct economic impact on American citizens. sources.headline: Israel has voted, but what comes next? Dissecting a messy ballot and coalition-building process
sources.text:
The Israeli election of Oct. 27, 2026, was among the most highly anticipated votes in the country’s history. It was consequential, if not yet conclusive.
With nearly all the votes counted, it is still unclear who will lead the country following the first national ballot since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, and the devastating wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran that Israel has launched since.
The Conversation turned to Dov Waxman, an expert on Israeli politics at the University of California, Los Angeles, to walk us through the main takeaways and the process and difficulties facing anyone trying to form a coalition government following a divided vote.
What can we take away from the election results?
The first thing to note is simply the massive turnout – with a 77.7% turnout of those eligible voting, the highest turnout in more than two decades. That in itself is significant. It underscores how much importance Israelis attached to this vote.
Before the election, many observers were saying that it was one of the most consequential – if not the most consequential – votes, and clearly many Israelis felt the same way.
What drove this high turnout was different types of fears. Israelis of all persuasions were worried about how the outcome would affect what kind of country Israel becomes.
The second big takeaway is that the ruling coalition, formed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after the 2022 election, was resoundingly rejected by the majority of Israeli voters – well over 50% cast their vote for parties opposed to the current government.
Likud supporters at an election night event in Jerusalem, Israel.
Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images
The five parties that make up Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious coalition went into the election with 68 seats in the 120-seat parliament. That same bloc will now have 53 – and that is a significant loss, no matter how Netanyahu tries to spin this as a victory.
It means that those five parties will not be able to form the next government, and as such, the vote stands as a repudiation of the Netanyahu government.
Netanyahu’s Likud party will still be the largest in parliament. But its share of the national vote declined, and it looks like it will have six fewer seats in the next parliament, another blow to Netanyahu.
Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners fared worse than expected, too. In part, this was due to “wasted votes” going to a new far-right party that failed to make it above the 3.25% of the national vote needed to be represented in parliament. Also, Likud drew some voters away from these far-right parties who had voted for them in the last election.
What drove the Arab parties’ surprise showing?
The performance of the Arab majority parties – the more secular and left-wing Joint List and the more religious and conservative United Arab List – is very important.
Combined, they currently look to have increased their representation by nine seats, bringing their total to 19, a historic high for them.
The reason for that is the massive turnout of Arab voters – much higher than the last election. But also, a less noticed trend is the increase in Jewish votes that those parties received. It is important to note that these are Arab-majority parties, not simply Arab parties.
Israeli left-wing protesters call for the formation of a government including Arab parties.
Ilia Yefimovich/AFP via Getty Images
Aside from Netanyahu, it was also a disappointing result for the main opposition party, Yashar; its leader, Gadi Eisenkot; and the anti-Netanyahu Change Bloc it was part of. The preelection polls suggested that the Zionist opposition bloc would do slightly better than the ruling coalition bloc.
But Yashar ended up with over 200,000 fewer votes than Likud, winning a projected 21 seats compared to Likud’s 26, and the “Change Bloc” is heading to 48 seats, far short of a parliamentary majority.
Ultimately, what is clear is that the Israeli public remains deeply divided. And the fact that there is still a good chance that Netanyahu will emerge as prime minister is remarkable given that many observers had already written his political obituary after the Oct. 7 attack.
Was the vote a referendum on Netanyahu?
Certainly many saw this as a referendum on Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.
For his supporters, Netanyahu is the only person to be trusted with Israel’s security, especially given the threat from Iran. They credit him for weakening – albeit not defeating – the two non-state actors that most threaten Israeli security, Hezbollah and Hamas, and they praise him for ensuring President Donald Trump’s support for Israel.
But for those who voted against Netanyahu, the fact that he has refused to take any personal responsibility for the Oct. 7 security failure – amid reports that he had advance warning of a major planned Hamas attack – factored into his poor election showing, as did his government’s refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the Oct. 7 security failings.
Many also blame Netanyahu for not prioritizing the release of the Israeli hostages held in Gaza and prolonging the war there. He is also held responsible by many for the precipitous decline in Israel’s international standing and for jeopardizing Israel’s crucial alliance with the United States.
But it was domestic issues, rather than external ones, that motivated many of those who voted for anti-Netanyahu parties. Many fear that democracy in Israel is under attack, and they particularly oppose the effort by Netanyahu’s government to weaken the power and independence of the Israeli judiciary, which sparked massive street protests in 2023. They also strongly resent that Netanyahu’s government has allowed ultra-Orthodox men to avoid military service, despite the Israeli military’s growing manpower shortage. And on a personal level, Netanyahu is widely perceived as self-serving and dishonest – he is still on trial for corruption.
Arab voters have other, more specific concerns that drove them to vote in record numbers, in addition to the Netanyahu government’s policies in Gaza and the West Bank, which they strongly oppose. Chief among them is the soaring rates of violent crime in their communities, which the government – particularly the far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir, who oversees the police – has done nothing to address, say his critics. More broadly, many Palestinian-Arab citizens of Israel fear that if the far-right parties remained in power, their civil rights would be under threat.
What should we expect next?
The key thing to underline is what happens on election day in Israel is just the first stage in the process of forming a new government. Since no party ever receives a majority of seats in the parliament, what really matters is what happens after the election when the coalition building begins. This can take weeks, if not longer.
The party with the largest number of seats typically gets the first chance to assemble a governing coalition, but not always. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will choose who gets the first chance to form a government based on who is most likely to succeed.
Right now, it looks like Eisenkot will get the first opportunity, but his only real option is to form a minority government that would depend on the parliamentary support of the Arab-majority parties – which some members of his Change Bloc adamantly oppose.
Former Israeli military chief and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot waves an Israeli flag as he addresses supporters on Oct. 28, 2026.
Tomer Neuberg/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images
Despite the success of the Arab-majority parties in the election, it is unlikely they will be invited to be formal members of any coalition – although that has happened once in the past, when the United Arab List joined the short-lived government of 2021-22 led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
If Eisenkot is unable to form a government, then Netanyahu will get the chance. He could try to entice some leaders of the parties in the Change bloc to defect and join a right-wing government under his leadership, or a broader “national unity” government with a rotating leader. Netanyahu did that in the past with Benny Gantz, but then he later prevented Gantz from becoming prime minister – so I doubt Eisenkot would agree to do this with Netanyahu.
There are reports in the media that the Trump administration would like a national unity government in Israel, so that might increase the pressure on Eisenkot to accept this outcome. And should war with Iran heat up again, that would increase the pressure.
The most likely scenario, I believe, is that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot will be able to form a government, and a new election will be called, with Netanyahu as caretaker prime minister until that vote. Netanyahu has reason to hope that his bloc will do better in another election, so that may well be his game plan. In which case, it will be many months until Israel has a new government.

sources.headline: The Security Challenges Facing the Next Israeli Leader
sources.text:
Israel’s election results remain unclear, but whether current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu again emerges triumphant or a new government, perhaps led by Gadi Eisenkot, takes power, the country is at a crossroads. Although Israel has demonstrated its military power throughout the Middle East, it is trapped in endless conflict on multiple fronts, overstretched at home, and damaging its long-term relationship with the United States.
In the three years since Oct. 7, 2023, when a Hamas terrorist attack killed almost 1,200 Israelis, Israel’s regional military power has reached new heights. Not only did Israel smash Hamas after the attack, but it also took on the far more formidable Hezbollah, severely weakening its leadership, arsenal, and fighting forces in a continuing campaign. In 2025 and then again in 2026, Israel (along with the United States) attacked Iran, killing much of its senior leadership and setting back its nuclear program and military. In addition to striking its enemies, Israel now occupies around 70 percent of the Gaza Strip, large parts of Lebanon, and several miles along its border with Syria, using these buffer zones to guard against another Oct. 7-like attack and make it more difficult for terrorist groups to use drones, rockets, and other short-distance systems to strike Israel.

These conflicts, however, have brought with them additional problems for Israel that its new government must address. In particular, Israel has failed to translate military success into lasting strategic gains.
The Iran war is the most pressing security challenge. What was intended as a short war is now in its ninth month, with no end in sight—and indeed escalation seems possible. Although the United States is focused on the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz and the security of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and other Gulf allies, Israel is more concerned about Iran’s long-range missile arsenal and provision of drones and money to anti-Israel proxies, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, allowing the group to rearm.
More broadly, Israel must break the cycle of endless conflict. In the last three years, Israel has used military force in eight countries and territories: Gaza, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Qatar, Syria, the West Bank, and Yemen. Israel’s enemies, however, show no sign of folding, even as the populations they claim to represent suffer tremendously. Israel can degrade its enemies’ military capabilities, but it is far harder to stop them from rebuilding or get them to abandon their hostility. Iran may emerge from the war wounded but vengeful, and it may commit at least some of the resources it gains under any cease-fire agreement, such as the one the United States proposed in June, to countering Israel. Hamas and Hezbollah are far weaker, but Hamas is still the most important Palestinian actor in Gaza, and Hezbollah, too, remains formidable.
This lack of progress makes Israel’s wars unsustainable even as their human cost is staggering. In Lebanon, Iran, and the West Bank, Israeli operations have killed thousands of civilians as well as many enemy fighters, while the civilian figure for Gaza is in the tens of thousands. Israel has devastated infrastructure in Gaza and parts of Lebanon, with mass displacement in both areas. Even if the new Israeli government places little weight on this suffering, other countries do, and support for Israel is low in most of the world.
Israeli leaders may dismiss this general collapse in support as a necessary price to pay for its security, but it also shapes how key allies treat the country. Israel has long hoped to secure an alliance with Saudi Arabia, but this is politically impossible for Riyadh when the deaths of Palestinian children are a regular feature in the news.
Far more consequential are the effects on Israel’s relationship with the United States. Polling by the Pew Research Center indicates that only 16 percent of Democrats and 51 percent of Republicans have favorable views of the Israeli government. Among young adults, those figures are 12 percent for Democrats and only 28 percent for Republicans.
The United States supports Israel militarily, economically, and diplomatically, as well as being a partner in the Iran war. Even if most forms of support continue, the coming years could see increased congressional scrutiny of military assistance to Israel, less diplomatic support in the United Nations and elsewhere, and a possible decline in financial support.
Because the endless wars draw on Israeli reservists, they are also increasing strains in Israeli society. In addition to the risk of casualties, the reservists are away from their jobs and families for long stretches, with no end in sight. There is an Israeli joke that one-third of Israelis pay taxes, one-third work, and one-third serve in the military. The joke is that it is the same third, as Israel’s large Arab population and most of its ultra-Orthodox community do not serve. Reflecting this disproportionate burden, one contentious issue in the latest election was the question of whether Israel’s large and growing Haredi population should be forced to serve in the military.
Historically, Israel has excelled at operations and tactics while having a short-term, narrow mindset about how to achieve security in general. As one Israeli security official joked to me on a recent trip, “The Hebrew word for ‘strategy’ is ‘tactics.’” This mentality has helped Israel score impressive military victories over Hezbollah and Hamas, but it has also left Israel trapped in multiple endless wars with little hope of lasting security. The new Israeli government, whether led by Netanyahu, Eisenkot, or another figure, must translate military dominance into sustainable political arrangements. Otherwise, Israeli society risks exhaustion while the country loses vital international support.

sources.text:
Israel’s elections on Tuesday have delivered a parliament with no clear path to a new government. Incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party has won 27 out of 120 available seats in the Knesset, leaving his right-wing coalition short of the seats needed for a majority, and opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party has won 21 seats, also leaving it unable to form a government unless it joins forces with the surging Arab parties that his allies have previously refused to join forces with.
What happens next, and what will coalition bargaining reveal about where Israeli society stands, three years on from the devastating Hamas attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and the deadly regional wars that followed? On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Dahlia Scheindlin, an Israeli pollster and political scientist who is a columnist for Haaretz.
